summary: Creates richer, low-friction invitations to participate beyond the course, making more of King’s campuses while developing legitimate blended, digital and distance routes into student life for those who are less campus-present.
detailSummary:
Student life at King’s is rightly centred on the course, while participation in the broader life of a university brings important additional opportunities for connection, belonging and development. This deliverable will make more deliberate use of King’s expansive estate to support that experience, packing campuses with rich, low-friction invitations to connect, join in and encounter opportunities beyond scheduled study.

As patterns of student life change, this experience can no longer depend on students simply dwelling on campus and discovering what is available. King’s will use a deepening understanding of student needs, purposes, journeys and patterns of presence to design activity more intelligently around how students actually engage with the university, connecting belonging and community more deliberately with wider opportunity and graduate futures.

Physical presence will not be the price of admission to a rich King’s student life. Alongside a more compelling campus experience, King’s will grow thoughtful blended, digital and distance routes into participation beyond the course. Students should encounter authentic invitations to take part wherever they engage with King’s, accumulating relationships and experiences that build belonging and allow them to feel genuinely and legitimately part of university life.
problemSolved: King’s estate does not consistently draw students into rich participation beyond scheduled study, while students who are less campus-present can have thinner access to the relationships, communities and opportunities of university life.
whatChanges: King’s creates richer, low-friction physical and digital invitations into participation beyond the course, making more of its estate while building legitimate routes into student life for students who are less campus-present.

caseForChange.problem:
Student life at King’s is rightly centred on the course, but the broader university experience, and the benefits that flow from it, are also part of what students should be able to expect from university life. Much of that wider experience is created through the spaces, relationships, communities and opportunities that surround formal study. King’s has an expansive and exciting estate with significant potential to support this, but too often students arrive for scheduled activity and leave, missing the informal encounters and broader opportunities that deepen belonging and contribute to their perception of the value they receive from university.

But making campus richer cannot by itself ensure every student can access that wider experience. Students have very different capacities to spend additional time on campus, shaped by commuting, cost, paid work, caring responsibilities, disability, placements and patterns of study. If access to the wider King’s experience depends too heavily on physical presence, students with less flexibility risk unequal access to relationships, communities and opportunities that should form part of a King’s education.
caseForChange.opportunity:
King’s can pack its campuses with rich, low-friction activity that brings together connection, belonging, wider opportunity and graduate futures, informed by a deepening understanding of student needs and purposes, and by how students move through the estate and where they have capacity to engage.

Alongside this, King’s can design thoughtful blended, digital and distance equivalents that give students who are less campus-present meaningful access to the same broader benefits of university life, without simply trying to replicate the physical experience online.
caseForChange.whyNow:
The era of incidental dwelling on campus has changed. Commuting, paid work, caring responsibilities and financial pressure mean fewer students can simply spend unstructured time at university and discover the wider student experience by being there. If King’s wants campus to generate connection, community and opportunity, it increasingly needs to design for that deliberately.

This matters particularly because King’s has successfully widened participation, growing its commuting population, while also significantly expanding distance learning with ambitions to grow further. The challenge is therefore twofold: make the time students do spend on campus richer and more valuable, while creating thoughtful routes into the wider King’s experience for those who are less, or never, physically present.
caseForChange.intendedChange:
Students encounter frequent, low-friction invitations to join in as they move around campus and as they engage with King’s digitally. Spaces, activities and digital experiences are designed to draw students naturally into connection, community, wider opportunity and graduate futures, rather than relying on them to seek these things out for themselves.

These invitations work across different patterns of participation, enabling students to engage in ways that feel authentic to how they study and live. More students build relationships and a sense of belonging, while accumulating the experiences and participation that allow them to feel genuinely and legitimately part of university life at King’s.
